newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin says Russia stable, expects more investment.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin says Russia stable, expects more investment.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin said on Thursday Russia had reached political stability and he expected more foreign investment soon, Interfax news agency said.
"Investment into our country will come in increasing amounts because political stabilisation has installed itself in Russia," Interfax quoted Yeltsin as telling foreign ambassadors.
Interfax quoted him as saying that the period of crises in Russia had passed and that the next stage of reform -- economic growth -- was waiting its turn.

Yeltsin said Russia was energetically pushing forward reforms in many spheres, had created the basis for a "state of law", and started a massive military overhaul to convert the Soviet-era ineffective military machine into a compact professional force.

Russia has eliminated hyperinflation and has announced plans to redenominate the rouble by stripping three zeroes from the currency, crowning six years of tough economic reforms and signalling confidence that soaring prices and a tumbling rouble are history.
The Russian economy shrank about five percent in 1996 and ministers say gross domestic product could fall up to two percent again this year, but there are signs of growth in the economy already.
However, many important reforms such as a new tax code are still on the drawing board, largely due to resistance from Russia's opposition-dominated parliament.
Millions of Russians are not receiving their wages on time and many live below the official poverty line.
Public dissatisfaction with reforms benefits the Kremlin's political opponents, mainly communists and nationalists, who have promised a wave of public outcry in the autumn.
Yeltsin also said Russia was an advocate of partnership and co-operation between all countries, and urged a halt to all armed conflicts.
"We are for a peaceful settlement of all conflicts in the Caucasus, Afghanistan, the Middle East, and the region of the Great African Lakes," Yeltsin said.
